messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena, a 59-year-old project manager, was taken captive during a robbery at the office two years ago. For three days she was bound to a chair in a storage room, her neck strained against the ropes, with no way out and no one hearing her calls. The physical pain and utter helplessness of that locked space imprinted themselves on her. Now, any reminder of entrapment—a conference room door that sticks, a crowded elevator, the familiar ache in her neck—immediately sets off a visceral alarm. At home, she finds herself scanning doorways and windows, unable to relax even when she knows she is safe. She often startles at ordinary sounds, reacting as if danger is present when nothing is wrong. These triggers also shatter the fragile distance she tries to keep from the event. When the neck pain flares or she feels boxed in, she is flooded with the belief that she has lost the happiness she once had, that she is now numb and hollow, and that anyone could turn out to be a threat. She has come to believe that you can never really know who will harm you, and this conviction keeps her perpetually on guard, alert even in her own home. That constant vigilance, in turn, makes her hyperaware of any confined space or physical tension; she notices locked doors she would have ignored before, and the neck ache feels like a warning. In response to this ever-present threat, Elena resorts to mind games she knows are not rational. She tells herself the captivity did not really happen or was not that bad—a kind of magical thinking that briefly lifts the weight. But she cannot stop herself from going over and over the details, trying to make sense of what she could have done differently. She dwells on her own actions, convinced she must have made a mistake. These strategies only deepen her despair: the rumination reinforces her sense that she is broken, that the happy person she used to be is gone, and that emotional numbness is her permanent state. And because the overanalysing never yields an answer, the threat never resolves—she remains keyed up, ready for the next false alarm. The cycle tightens over months. She avoids meetings in windowless rooms, claiming scheduling conflicts, and has stopped visiting her daughter’s apartment because the hallway is narrow. The neck pain itself has become a trigger she cannot escape; every time she feels it, she is back in the chair. She has lost touch with old friends, explaining that she is too tired, but really she cannot bear to be in unfamiliar spaces. What finally brings Elena to therapy is her daughter’s concern: Elena jumped at the sound of a door clicking shut and then spent an hour replaying the robbery, asking herself why she had not fought harder. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again, and she is desperate to find a way out of the locked room her mind has become.
